item.question: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, ... Why does the rule take every one of them to 1?
item.question_tex: $1$, $2$, $4$, $8$, $16$, $32$, $64$, ... Why does the rule take every one of them to $1$?

item.question: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, ... Why does the rule take every one of them to 1?
steps_tex: The numbers $1$, $2$, $4$, $8$, $16$, $32$, $64$, ... are the powers of $2$: each is double the one before it.
Apart from $1$, every one of them is even, so the rule halves it.
Halving a power of $2$ gives the power of $2$ before it: half of $64$ is $32$, half of $32$ is $16$, and so on.
So each step moves one place back along the list: $64$, $32$, $16$, $8$, $4$, $2$, $1$.
No odd number appears before $1$, so the rule never has to multiply by $3$ and add $1$.
So the sequence keeps moving back along the list until it reaches $1$; for example $64$ takes $6$ steps.
item.answer_tex: Every power of $2$ except $1$ is even, so the rule halves it and moves one place back along the list. No odd number appears on the way, so it always reaches $1$.
